nameStory: The Green Hydra gets its vibrant name from its distinctive emerald coloration, which comes from tiny green algae called Chlorella that live right inside its body cells. Unlike other hydras that are typically clear or brownish, this little freshwater animal literally glows green thanks to its microscopic plant partners.
description: Green Hydras are tiny freshwater animals that look like miniature sea anemones, typically about 10mm long (roughly the size of your pinky nail). They have a tube-like body topped with a ring of slender tentacles that are about half their body length. What makes them special is their brilliant green color, which comes from algae living inside their cells. These simple but fascinating creatures belong to the same group as jellyfish and corals, despite living in ponds and streams.

idTips.label: Bright Green Color
idTips.description: The unmistakable emerald green coloration throughout the body and tentacles, created by symbiotic algae living within the animal's cells

idTips.label: Tentacle Crown
idTips.description: Ring of 6-10 thin, flexible tentacles around the mouth that wave gently in the water and can contract instantly when touched

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Small tube-like body about 10mm long (pinky nail sized) that can stretch and contract like a tiny accordion

idTips.label: Attachment Behavior
idTips.description: Typically found firmly attached to aquatic plants, rocks, or debris by a sticky basal disc, feeling slightly slimy to the touch

idTips.label: Movement Pattern
idTips.description: Usually stays in one spot but can slowly glide along surfaces or do a distinctive somersaulting motion when disturbed

habitat: Look for Green Hydras in still or slow-moving freshwater like ponds, quiet stream pools, and lake edges throughout New England. They prefer areas with aquatic vegetation where they can attach to submerged plant stems, leaves, or underwater rocks. You'll often find them in shallow, sunlit areas where their algae partners can photosynthesize effectively.

seasonality.spring: Active and easy to spot as water warms up, often found attached to emerging aquatic vegetation in shallow areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when their green color is most vibrant due to active photosynthesis by their algae partners. Best time for observation.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may appear less vibrant as algae activity decreases with shorter daylight hours and cooling water.
seasonality.winter: Survive under ice in dormant state or as resistant buds, rarely visible to casual observers during coldest months.

funFact: Green Hydras have essentially turned themselves into living solar panels by hosting algae inside their cells - the algae make food from sunlight while the hydra provides protection, creating a partnership so successful that the hydra actually suppresses its own immune system to keep its algae roommates happy and healthy.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other hydra species, but the bright green color makes Green Hydras unmistakable - other hydras are typically clear, white, or brownish. If it's not green, it's not a Green Hydra!
contextualKnowledge: Despite their plant-like appearance and green color, hydras are actually animals closely related to jellyfish and sea anemones. The 'Hydra' name comes from the mythical Greek monster that could regrow its heads - fitting since these animals can regenerate lost body parts and even reproduce by budding off tiny clones.
compareHints: While there are other green hydra species in the broader family, Hydra viridissima is the primary green hydra found in New England waters. Other hydra species in the region lack the distinctive green coloration and symbiotic algae partnership. The green color is your best field mark - no other common freshwater cnidarian in New England shares this bright emerald appearance.
